definition: Not yet settled or final, and likely to be changed or confirmed later.
example: The museum set a tentative opening date in early spring, pending the final safety inspection.
nuance: Tentative stresses uncertainty and openness to revision; provisional stresses a temporary stand-in until something permanent replaces it.
prompt: A club is scheduling a meeting before it knows when all its members are free.
options: They picked a tentative date of Thursday and asked everyone to confirm by Monday.
The tentative date was carved into the calendar as fixed, with no changes allowed.
The tentative organizer refused to give up and kept insisting on Thursday no matter what.
The date turned tentative the moment all ten members confirmed they could attend.
reasons: A date chosen while waiting for confirmation is still open to change.
Something locked in for good is final, the reverse of what the word describes.
Stubborn persistence is tenacity, a look-alike word; this one suggests uncertainty.
Full confirmation removes doubt, so it would make the date settled, not uncertain.

practice.prompt: A researcher presents early findings from a small study.
options: The tentative audience leaned forward and hung on every detail of her slides.
She proudly announced her tentative results as the final word on the subject.
She called her conclusions tentative because only twelve people had taken part so far.
She called her conclusions tentative because dozens of later studies had confirmed them.
reasons: Close, eager focus is attentiveness; this word is about doubt, not concentration.
Results presented as the last word are claimed as certain, not open to revision.
A tiny sample means the results could easily shift, so calling them unsettled fits.
Repeated confirmation makes findings firm, which contradicts calling them uncertain.
